item.research_question: Do high-entropy alloys (HEAs) possess unique irradiation damage resistance mechanisms compared to conventional alloys, and what are the specific roles of thermal conductivity, defect mobility, and defect energetics in this behavior?
item.material_system: Concentrated solid-solution alloys and HEAs (defined as alloys with ≥5 components at 5–35 at.%) including NiFe, NiCo, NiCoCrFe, CrFeCoNi, Ni0.8Fe0.2, Ni0.8Cr0.2, Fe-Cr, Fe-Ni, and CrFeCoNiMn; compared against pure Ni, pure Fe, and conventional austenitic steels.
item.processing_route: Not stated (Review of existing literature and atomistic simulations; no new processing described).
item.test_conditions: Irradiation with energetic neutrons (≥1 MeV), protons, or heavy ions; temperatures ranging from room temperature to high homologous temperatures (T/Tm > 0.2); damage levels up to 250 dpa; PKA energies ≥10 keV; specific mention of 14.1 MeV fusion neutrons and Gen-IV fission conditions (>600 °C).
key_findings: MD studies on NiFe (lower thermal conductivity) found significantly fewer stable Frenkel pair (FP) defects after cascades at PKA energies ≥10 keV compared to pure Ni.
In CrFeCoNi, void swelling was negligible between 16 and 54 dpa, with significant swelling only observed at high doses of 86–250 dpa.
Defect clusters in concentrated Ni binaries were found to be smaller and more numerous than in pure Ni at room temperature, attributed to slower defect mobilities.
Damage accumulation in pure Ni saturates earlier, whereas damage in concentrated alloys accumulates more slowly but may peak at a higher level at higher doses.
Void swelling in concentrated alloys is often suppressed by over an order of magnitude compared to pure metals at the same damage level.
Atomistic simulations show a distribution of migration energies in concentrated alloys, with average migration energies for interstitials being higher than in pure Ni.
A comprehensive review by Dąbrowa and Danielewski found no conclusive experimental evidence that thermally-induced diffusion is sluggish in HEAs compared to conventional alloys.
Some studies suggest HEAs may be 'self-healing' due to rapid recrystallization following cascade-induced amorphization caused by high inter-atomic stress levels.
item.mechanism: The authors describe a complex interplay of mechanisms: (1) Reduced thermal conductivity in HEAs leads to more localized thermal spikes, potentially allowing more FP recombination; (2) Sluggish defect mobilities (due to variable chemical environments and lattice distortion) reduce the migration of interstitials, bringing their mobility closer to vacancies, which suppresses void swelling and radiation-induced segregation; (3) Higher vacancy formation energies and distribution of defect formation energies in concentrated alloys contribute to void suppression; (4) High inter-atomic stresses may facilitate amorphization followed by rapid recrystallization ('self-healing').
item.limitations: The authors state that understanding of HEA irradiation responses remains in its infancy, with many proposed mechanisms (sluggish diffusion, lattice distortion) being unconvincing or not universally applicable. There is a lack of systematic studies comparing FCC, BCC, and HCP metals under identical conditions, and no conclusive experimental evidence for abnormally sluggish diffusion or lattice distortion in stable HEAs.
item.future_work: The authors highlight the need for more work to match the understanding of HEAs to that of conventional alloys, specifically calling for systematic studies comparing different crystal structures under the same irradiation conditions, and distinguishing between changes in defect migration energies versus formation energies during irradiation.
quotes: It is found that our understanding of the irradiation responses of HEAs remains in its infancy, and much work is needed in order for our knowledge of any single HEA system to match our understanding of conventional alloys such as austenitic steels.

A number of studies have suggested that HEAs possess 'special' irradiation damage resistance, although some of the proposed mechanisms, such as those based on sluggish diffusion and lattice distortion, remain somewhat unconvincing.

The results of atomistic simulations suggest this is indeed the case—there is a distribution of migration energies in concentrated alloys, and on average the migration energies are higher for interstitials and interstitial clusters in Ni alloys versus pure Ni.

item.research_question: Do High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) possess enhanced intrinsic damage resistance versus conventional alloys under irradiation, and what are the specific mechanisms or limitations governing their phase stability and mechanical response?
item.material_system: Al0.3CoCrFeNi, Al0.12NiCoFeCr, TiZrNbHfTa, CrFeNi-based alloys, CrFeMnCoNi, BCC refractory HEAs (Ti, V, Cr, Mn, Fe, Ta, W combinations), Fe-Ni-Mn-Cr, Fe-Cr-Ni austenitic alloys, 316 stainless steel, 316H stainless steel, 304 stainless steel, RAFM steel, MoNbTiTaW, CoCrFeNiPd, FeCuCrMnMo
item.processing_route: Not stated (text reviews existing studies involving thin films, nanocrystalline materials, arc melting, spark plasma sintering, and various irradiation conditions including He-irradiation, electron irradiation, and ion/neutron irradiation)
item.test_conditions: Irradiation at room temperature and 300-500 °C; thermal annealing at irradiation temperatures; damage levels up to many dpa; thin film and nanocrystalline conditions; He-irradiation; electron irradiation
key_findings: In Al0.3CoCrFeNi, ballistic mixing suppressed precipitation at lower temperatures while radiation-enhanced diffusion enhanced it at higher temperatures.
In Al0.12NiCoFeCr, irradiation led to decomposition of the single phase solid solution, whereas longer thermal exposure at 500 °C did not.
Moschetti et al. found a small increase (~10%) in nanohardness, yield strength, and ultimate-tensile strength for He-irradiated TiZrNbHfTa with no loss of ductility.
CrFeNi-based alloys showed significant hardening similar to 316 stainless steel, unlike BCC refractory HEAs which showed no or very limited hardening.
A sigma to BCC transition at room temperature has been observed in some alloys, which is very unlikely to have been favourable in the non-irradiated state.
The dose needed for damage saturation in an Fe-Ni-Mn-Cr alloy was found to be comparable to that in more conventional Fe-Cr-Ni austenitic alloys at 500 °C.
Microstructural evolution and irradiation hardening in some FCC HEAs was found to be similar to 316H stainless steel at 300 °C.
CrFeMnCoNi retained more hydrogen than 304 and 316 L steels but showed only marginal ductility decrease after gaseous charging.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that the disparity in responses between BCC and FCC HEAs may be due to the distribution of migration energies for vacancies and interstitials exhibiting a much larger overlap in BCC HEAs, leading to enhanced defect recombination. They suggest that compositional complexity might uniquely enable effects such as poor thermal conductivities affecting cascade dynamics (reducing FPs formed) and a spread in defect formation energies (potentially higher vacancy formation energies).
item.limitations: Many studies fail to assess alloys under conditions that appropriately probe resistance to irradiation damage, such as using thin films where defects annihilate at surfaces, nanocrystalline materials with many boundaries, irradiation at room temperature where defect mobility is inhibited, or electron irradiation which does not cause the same damage as ions or neutrons. Additionally, there is a lack of comparison to conventional alloys or less compositionally-complex alloys assessed under the same conditions.
item.future_work: Further investigation is needed into the disparity in responses of BCC vs. FCC HEAs, the influence of diffusion and lattice distortion, the effect of reduced thermal conductivities on cascade dynamics, and the defect energetics in BCC refractory HEAs. Design efforts require tuning compositions to optimize defect formation energies, sink strengths, and biases using advanced atomic-scale models.
quotes: ballistic mixing suppressed precipitation in irradiated areas in comparison to non-irradiated regions, but radiation-enhanced diffusion was found to enhance it at higher temperatures
the distribution of migration energies for vacancies and interstitials exhibiting a much larger overlap in BCC HEAs compared to FCC HEAs, leading to enhanced defect recombination
their concentrated compositions are more likely to result in poor thermal conductivities, and this may affect the short-term damage evolution immediately following the cascade
